messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Vignette:
The event itself had no order. That was the part that Frank could never straighten out, no matter how many times he went over it in his head. He had been stationed at the forward aid station, a reinforced concrete structure that should have been safe. The earthquake hit at 03:47. He remembered the sound first—a deep, grinding roar that came up through the floor and seemed to vibrate inside his bones. Then the lights went out. Then the ceiling came down. He was pinned for almost four hours, his pelvis trapped under a collapsed beam, the weight of the building pressing him into the rubble. He could hear the other men. One of them, a young private named Dawes, had been thrown clear but was buried up to his chest. Frank could hear him calling out, could hear his voice getting weaker, and he could not reach him. He could not move. He could not do his job. By the time the rescue teams dug him out, Dawes was silent. Frank had been a medic for seventeen years. He had never lost a man he could reach. He could not put the hours in the right order. He knew he had been trapped, and he knew he had been rescued, but the sequence of what happened between those two points—which screams came first, whether he had been conscious the whole time, whether he had tried to call out or had just lain there—was a tangle he could not straighten.

In the weeks that followed, Frank was evacuated stateside and spent a month in a medical unit for his physical injuries. He healed. The pelvis knitted. The bruises faded. But something else had broken that he could not name. He returned to his home in a quiet suburb outside Fort Bragg, and the silence was unbearable. He would sit in his living room, and the world felt flat, drained of all purpose. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. He had been a man who knew exactly who he was—a medic, a helper, a man who could walk into chaos and make it stop—and now he did not recognize himself. He would catch his reflection in the dark glass of the television and think, *Who is that?* His beliefs about how the world worked, the quiet conviction that if you were competent and careful you could keep people safe, had been destroyed. He had been careful. He had been competent. And Dawes had died anyway.

His wife, Maria, had died of cancer three years before the earthquake. He had thought he understood loss. He had grieved her, had moved through it, had found a way to go on. But this was different. This was not grief. This was a dismantling. He stopped going to the gym. He stopped answering calls from his old unit. He stopped cooking—what was the point of a meal for one? He would sit in the dark and listen to the house settle, and every creak of the floorboards, every distant car door slamming, every sudden thud from the neighbor's yard would send a spike of adrenaline through his chest. His heart would hammer, his palms would sweat, and he would be back under that beam, the weight of the building on his lungs. The sound of a garbage truck backing up, with its beeping alarm, would hit him like a physical blow. A dropped pan in the kitchen would make him lurch to his feet, fists clenched, scanning for a threat that was not there. He knew, intellectually, that he was safe. He was in his own home. There was no earthquake. There was no collapsing building. But knowing did not help. His body did not believe it.

He grew hypervigilant. He would scan parking lots before getting out of his car. He would note the exits in every room he entered. He would avoid any space with a low ceiling—basements, storage rooms, the walk-in pantry at the grocery store. He stopped going to the hardware store because the aisles were narrow and the shelving units loomed overhead, and he could feel the weight of them, could feel them falling. At work, he had been reassigned to administrative duties while he recovered, but he could not concentrate. A colleague would walk up behind him and he would flinch, hard, his breath catching. He started working from home, then stopped working altogether. The medical leave became indefinite. He told himself he just needed time. But time was not helping.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a night in late October. A thunderstorm rolled in around midnight. The first crack of thunder was so loud it rattled the windows. Frank was on the floor before he knew he had moved, curled in the corner of the hallway, his hands over his head, his whole body shaking. The terror was as fresh as it had been under the rubble—the same taste of dust and copper, the same pressure in his chest, the same certain knowledge that he was about to die. He stayed there for twenty minutes, until the storm passed, and when he finally stood up, he looked at himself in the mirror and did not know the man staring back. He called the VA the next morning. He told the intake nurse he could not keep living this way. He did not say what he really feared: that he had already stopped living, that he was just occupying space, waiting for something he could not name. He said he wanted to feel like himself again. He was not sure that was possible, but he was willing to try.
